hints: Start from what part of haemoglobin actually holds oxygen - remember it is not the amino acid chain itself but a small non-protein part tucked inside each subunit.
Think about numbers - how many subunits and oxygen-binding sites are there in one whole molecule, and how does binding the first oxygen make the next ones easier?
Link the iron-containing group to reversible binding and the change in shape that helps quick loading in the lungs and unloading in tissues.
walkthrough:
The Oxygen-Carrying Part Is Haem With Iron**
Each of the four polypeptide chains in haemoglobin holds one haem group, which is a prosthetic group. At the centre of each haem is one iron atom, and this is the exact site where one oxygen molecule binds reversibly.

Four Sites Means Four Oxygens Per Molecule**
Because there are four haems per haemoglobin molecule, one haemoglobin can carry four oxygen molecules at full saturation. That multiplies the amount of oxygen carried in blood compared to simple diffusion in plasma.

Cooperative Binding Makes Loading and Unloading Efficient**
When the first oxygen binds, it slightly changes the shape of the whole molecule. This makes it easier for the second and third oxygens to bind, and the same in reverse for release. This cooperative effect allows rapid loading where oxygen is plentiful and rapid unloading where it is needed.

Final answer: Each haemoglobin molecule has four haem groups, each containing one iron atom. Each iron binds one oxygen molecule reversibly, so four oxygen molecules per haemoglobin. Binding shows cooperativity - binding of first oxygen changes shape to make further binding easier, allowing efficient loading and unloading.

hints: Picture how a globular protein folds up into a compact ball - think about where different types of amino acid R groups end up in that ball.
Remember that water is polar, so which type of R groups on the surface will interact well with water and what bond forms with water?
walkthrough:
Folding Puts Water-Loving Groups On The Outside**
The globin chains fold into precise tertiary structures and then assemble into a quaternary structure. Folding tucks hydrophobic R groups into the centre and leaves hydrophilic R groups exposed on the surface.

Surface Groups Bond To Water**
The exposed hydrophilic R groups attract water molecules and form hydrogen bonds with them. That interaction with water all around the molecule keeps haemoglobin dissolved in the cytoplasm of red blood cells and in plasma.

Final answer: Polypeptide chains fold to give globular tertiary and quaternary structure with hydrophilic R groups on the outside. These form hydrogen bonds with surrounding water molecules, so haemoglobin is soluble.

hints: Find $6.4 \text{ kPa}$ on the x-axis of Fig. 6.1, go straight up to each curve and then straight across to the y-axis to read percentage saturation.
walkthrough:
Read Across From 6.4 kPa**
Locate $6.4 \text{ kPa}$ on the partial pressure axis. Move vertically up to meet the llama curve, then horizontally to the saturation axis to get about $90.5\%$. Do the same for the lower human curve to get about $78.5\%$.

hints: Recall what left and right mean on a dissociation curve - at any same x-value, which curve gives higher saturation and what word describes that attraction for oxygen?
Connect this to life at 3500 m where air has a low partial pressure of oxygen, and think about why picking up more oxygen in the lungs helps respiration in tissues.
walkthrough:
Left Means Higher Affinity**
A curve to the left means that at any given partial pressure, for example $6.4 \text{ kPa}$, saturation is higher - $90.5\%$ versus $78.5\%$. That shows llama haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen and holds onto it more strongly.

Advantage Where Oxygen Is Scarce**
At high altitude the partial pressure of oxygen in air and lungs is low. Higher affinity lets llamas still load a large amount of oxygen in the lungs despite the low pressure, so enough oxygen can be transported in blood and delivered to respiring tissues.

Final answer: At high altitude partial pressure of oxygen is low. Left-shifted curve means higher affinity for oxygen, so at the same low partial pressure haemoglobin is more saturated. This allows sufficient oxygen uptake in lungs for delivery to tissues for respiration.
